prompt: Hypothetical: the rule is to withdraw only when equity is at a new high-water mark and above Rs 60,000 (starting capital Rs 50,000 plus Rs 10,000). After one good month, equity is Rs 55,000. Can the trader withdraw?

options.text: Yes. One good month is enough.
No. Rs 55,000 is below Rs 60,000, so the threshold is not met.
Yes, if the trader takes only 5% of the gain.
Yes, because Rs 55,000 is a new high-water mark.

explanations.a: Wrong. One good month does not meet the threshold. The rule requires both a new high and a level above Rs 60,000.
explanations.c: Wrong. A partial withdrawal still needs the threshold to be met first. Rs 55,000 is below Rs 60,000.
explanations.d: Wrong. Rs 55,000 is a new high-water mark, but the rule also requires equity above Rs 60,000.

prompt: Hypothetical: equity is Rs 53,000 and the high-water mark is Rs 57,000. The trader wants to withdraw Rs 5,000 for a household bill. Which response fits the rules?

options.text: Withdraw. It is the trader's money, so the account can take the loss.
Do not withdraw. Withdrawals during a drawdown are not allowed, because they lower the base the account must recover.
Withdraw if the bill is urgent, then top up the account later.
Withdraw, because a withdrawal under 10% of equity is always allowed.

explanations.a: Wrong. The account is in drawdown. A withdrawal makes the gap to the high-water mark harder to recover, and the threshold is not met.
explanations.c: Wrong. An urgent need does not change the rule. A later top-up from household money breaks the rule that household money is never trading capital.
explanations.d: Wrong. No percentage limit makes a withdrawal allowed in a drawdown. The threshold and the high-water condition both have to be met.

prompt: Statement: 'My account is 7% below its high-water mark, so I will add Rs 20,000 of household savings to get back to the peak faster.' Which part is the mistake?

options.text: Adding household savings to a losing account. Household money is never trading capital.
Treating the high-water mark as a target to reach quickly.
Nothing. A top-up is fine when the account is recovering.

explanations.a: Wrong. Being below the high-water mark is a measured fact. Its size is what the drawdown rule reads.
explanations.c: Wrong. The high-water mark is a reference point. Wanting to reach it quickly is pressure to act. But the clear error here is the money source (see b).
explanations.d: Wrong. A top-up from household money breaks the capital-first rules, whether or not the account is recovering (see *Capital allocation*).

prompt: Hypothetical: the equity path is Rs 50,000, 54,000, 51,000, 57,000, 53,000. What is the drawdown from the high-water mark at the end, in percent?
solution: The high-water mark is the highest value so far, 57,000. Drawdown = (57,000 - 53,000) / 57,000 = 4,000 / 57,000 = 0.0702, which is 7.0%. Check: 57,000 x 7.0% = 3,990, close to 4,000.

prompt: Hypothetical: the trader has lost 15% and wants to raise risk per trade from 1% to 2% to win the loss back faster. Is this allowed?

options.text: Yes. Recovering faster is the purpose of the account.
No. Increasing size after losses is a capital-first rule break, and it speeds up the drawdown.
Yes, if the stop is tighter.

explanations.a: Wrong. Higher risk after a loss makes each further loss bigger. It does not make recovery more likely.
explanations.c: Wrong. A tighter stop does not offset a larger position. The risk per trade is still raised after losses.
explanations.d: Wrong. One winning trade does not reset the rule. Scale-up follows gates and recorded results, not a single trade.
